schools.summary: Clarke (following Usher) and Wesley reckon 'the thirty-sixth year' from the division of the kingdoms; Wesley's arithmetic (17+3+15) yields the thirty-five of the prior notice.
Henry confesses himself 'quite at a loss'; he reports the reckoning-from-the-division view but leans to Josephus's twenty-sixth year and a transcriber's error.
Ellicott judges the figures irreconcilable and prefers textual emendation ('thirty-six' a slip for sixteen or twenty-six), calling the 'kingdom of Judah' theory absurd.
Gill states the difficulty (Baasha dead a decade before) and defers to his notes on Kings.

debates.question: How can 'the six and thirtieth year' be reconciled with Baasha's death in Asa's twenty-sixth year?

sides.position: Reckon the year from the division of the kingdoms (the 'kingdom of Judah'), coinciding with Asa's sixteenth year
A textual corruption — 'thirty-six' a scribal slip for sixteen or twenty-six

outliers.note: Dismisses the ancient 'kingdom of Judah' reckoning as flatly 'absurd,' since the Hebrew idiom always denotes a king's reign.

schools.summary: Keil notes vv.1-6 agree almost verbatim with Kings; Ellicott marks the abridgement, the 'purposely weakened' statement, the dropped pedigree of Benhadad, and the Aramaizing 'Darmeseq.'
Henry: rifling the temple treasury to hire a heathen ally was a great aggravation of the sin — 'Must the temple be plundered to serve his carnal politics?'
Clarke reads 'there is a league' as an offensive-and-defensive treaty between the two kings.
Ellicott confirms 'berith,' a covenant, and notes the verse stands almost verbatim as 1 Kings 15:19 with minute changes ('depart' = 'go up').
Henry lays a threefold fault: a league with a heathen king, valuing it above his covenant with God, and hiring Benhadad to break faith with Baasha for a bribe.
Keil and Ellicott identify Abel-maim with Abel-Beth-Maachah and read the Chronicle's 'store cities of Naphtali' as a paraphrase of the Kings reading 'all Cinneroth.'
Henry makes Asa answerable for the blood and spoil of Benhadad's raid — 'the beginning of sin is as the letting forth of water.'
Ellicott reads 'let his work cease' (against Kings' 'dwelt in Tirzah') as a manuscript fault yielding a tautologous phrase; Keil notes the war-account agrees almost literally with Kings.
Henry: Benhadad's northern onslaught diverted Baasha from building Ramah to defending his own land.
Gill defers to the fuller narrative already related in Kings.
Ellicott: the chronicler smooths Kings' 'none was exempted,' notes Kings' 'Geba of Benjamin,' and ties Mizpah to the cistern of Jeremiah 41:9.
Clarke reads 'took all Judah' as the general levy for the work (cf. 1 Kings 15:22).
Henry: Asa seized Ramah's very materials and turned them to his own use, building Geba and Mizpah from the spoil.
Gill defers to the parallel narrative.

Keil places Hanani as father of Jehu son of Hanani; Ellicott notes 'the seer' (ha-roeh) points to an ancient source and that Hanani's words accord with the greater prophets — the alliance forfeited a victory over the combined Israel-and-Syria host.
Clarke: the alliance thwarted providence's intended victory over Syria; Wesley: Benhadad is now reserved as a scourge, whereas an unbought war would have overthrown both Israel and Syria.
Henry: the king's greatest fault was relying on Syria and not on the LORD — God is displeased when distrusted and an arm of flesh preferred.
Gill: Hanani was sent of God to reprove the king.
Ellicott makes Zerah's Cushite-Libyan host the confirmation of v.7 (Zerah master of Egypt; the chronicler's own Hebrew and fuller sources); Keil reads the verse as the ground of the promise in v.9.
Gill reckons the former host at a million men and three hundred chariots, the Lubim being Libyans or Nubians.
Wesley identifies the Lubim as Libyans of Africa, or a kindred Arabian people.
Henry: Asa acted against his own experience — the many mercies received only aggravate present distrust.
Ellicott renders 'For Jehovah, his eyes run' (cf. Zech. 4:10, Job 1:7), notes the chronicler's favourite verb, and warns that peace bought by policy will not last (cf. Ahaz, 2 Chron. 28:20).
Wesley: a broken reed versus the rock of ages, 'perfect' meaning a sincerity Asa's heart here lacked; Clarke marks the threatened wars fulfilled (1 Kings 15:32).
Henry unfolds the quick-sighted, far-reaching eye of Providence — God governs in wisdom, for his people's good, protecting the upright.
Gill: the eyes of omniscience and of providential mercy are everywhere at once.
Keil and Ellicott render 'prison house' as a torture-stock (mahpecheth) and read the oppression as the violent crushing of Hanani's sympathisers (cf. Ahab and Micaiah).
Henry: 'Is this Asa?' — a good man in a rage, passing from persecuting the prophet to crushing his subjects; most persecutors have been tyrants.
Gill: the king's wrath at the reproof was another instance of his sin and folly.
Clarke: instead of humbling himself Asa persecuted the messenger, his heart hardened through sin's deceitfulness.

Keil marks the closing formula (cf. 1 Kings 15:23-24); Ellicott shows that Kings' notice of Asa's 'might' and 'cities' corroborates the chronicler's fuller account of the defences and Zerah's invasion.
Gill defers to the parallel in Kings.

Keil takes 'sought' as construed for consulting an oracle/idols — a godless trust, not the mere use of physicians; Ellicott sees Asa, like Ahaziah, preferring magical 'healers' (amulets, charms) to consulting Jehovah, and notes 'exceeding great' as the chronicler's own phrase.
Henry: the gout answered his sin (stocks for stocks); using physicians was his duty, trusting them his folly.
Wesley: the help of every creature must be used with an eye to the Creator; Clarke (with the Targum): he sought not discipline from the LORD's face but from physicians.
Gill: the gout was a just retaliation for the prophet's stocked feet; some think the physicians were conjurers.

debates.question: Were the 'physicians' Asa sought ordinary healers wrongly trusted, or heathen and magical practitioners consulted instead of God?

sides.position: Lawful physicians whose lawful use became sinful only through misplaced trust
Heathen/magical 'healers' (charms, amulets, conjurers) — an idolatry of the sickbed
holders: some (as reported by Gill and Henry)

schools.summary: Ellicott notes Kings gives no regnal figure here (only the 41 years of 1 Kings 15:10), the chronicler carrying the number to the death-notice; Keil marks the Chronicle's fuller, more exact account of the burial.
Gill: 'slept with his fathers' means simply he died.

themes: dignity of the house of David

schools.summary: Ellicott: the tomb hewn for himself (cf. Isa. 22:16), the spices and Aramaic vocabulary, the 'burning' of aromatic woods usual at royal obsequies — and no ground for reading blame into the splendour (against Zöckler).
Clarke thinks the body itself was burnt on a funeral pyre (with Virgil's parallel); Wesley reads the burning as of precious spices, a token of respect.
Henry: not vanity but the people's respect — 'let their faults be buried in their graves, while their services are remembered.'
Gill notes the family vault of many cells.

debates.question: Was the 'very great burning' the cremation of Asa's body, or only the burning of spices?

sides.position: The body itself was burnt on a funeral pyre heaped with spices and woods
Only aromatic spices and woods were burned, in the king's honour, not the body

debates.question: Was the lavish funeral an instance of Asa's vanity or an honour paid by his people?

sides.position: An honour and mark of the people's respect, notwithstanding his failings
An instance of vanity, a Gentile-like or Pharaoh-like pomp
